meta.notes: Source of truth for the history layer. Frames are snapshots, not a continuous scrub: the archives support dated moments, not annual geometry. Dot anchors are [lon, lat] EPSG:4326 and the site projects them, same as trivia. A frame's verified flag describes the frame's own words; each event card carries its own, so an uncertain detail flags itself without casting doubt on the plate around it. ship:false frames appear on the scrubber and say they are still being inked.
honesty_footnotes: Past market footprints are drawn with today's utility shapes. Distribution boundaries move far less than market membership, but this is an approximation.

The county layer is a hand trace of the FTC's own plate, Map III, dated 1925 and drawn on modern county equivalents. It shows fields of operation, which is where a group ran utilities, not where it held stock. Uncertainty is kept rather than resolved: about one county in nine is visibly filled but its pattern cannot be read, and ambiguous counties name both candidates. The plate also cannot carry city-scale operators, because Map IV states in its own margin that separate cities and towns served are not shown and the same applies to Map III. Richmond, Norfolk, Baltimore and Washington are the known cases.

The line between the Eastern and Western grids is drawn from today's utility service boundaries, assigned by balancing authority. It settled roughly here by the mid-1970s. In three places, near Scottsbluff, Miles City and Rapid City, one utility's single shape spans the line, so the line there is the best this source can support rather than a surveyed border.

Market footprints are built by replaying 34 dated events from 1996 and requiring every utility's final state to match the live map. Where a market's founding roster survives in filings, which is PJM, a utility named nowhere follows the named zone nearest it. Where it does not, a utility not named in any event is drawn as a member from that market's founding. 185 utilities out of 1,956, 9.5 per cent, would land in a different market on the 1999 or 2005 plate under their second or third nearest zone. They are municipals and co-ops in Ohio, Indiana and Kentucky, in the gaps between the companies PJM absorbed between 2004 and 2012, and all of them agree by 2014.

The 1999 plate draws five markets because five were running. MISO's 1998 approval was conditional, its compliance order came in April 1999, and it did not operate until December 2001. SPP did not become an RTO until 2004. Neither is drawn rather than being approximated.
meta.dots_note: The 50 largest urban places of the 1900 Census, every one of which had central-station service, plus four small places that were firsts. Populations are read from the Census table, not transcribed. Generated by pipeline/11-build-timeline-dots.mjs.
meta.seam_note: Regions and both boundaries are built by pipeline/13-build-seam.mjs, which places twenty independently known cities in the right machine before it writes the file.
meta.membership_note: Built by pipeline/15-build-membership.mjs from membership-events.json, which carries the per-market rule and the reason for it. PJM is the regression test: ten founding zones plus eleven later joins reproduce its present-day zones with no residue.

frames.title: Local power stations
frames.body: Electricity reached cities before it connected the country. Each glowing dot marks a city with a central power station. Most stations served only nearby blocks. Homes beyond the local wires had no service. The United States had thousands of separate electric systems and no national grid.
frames.note: Early direct-current systems could not move electricity far without expensive copper losses. Alternating current and transformers later allowed power to travel farther.

legend.label: A city with its own power station

frames.title: Holding companies spread
frames.body: Local utilities were being gathered into national corporate groups. A holding company owned other companies. An operating utility ran power plants and wires. Each patterned county shows where one of twenty major groups operated a utility in 1925. Blank counties may still have had city utilities or companies omitted from the federal map.
frames.note: This is a hand trace of Federal Trade Commission Map III. The source shows fields of operation: counties where each group ran utilities. It does not show stock ownership or separately served cities. Unclear hatch patterns remain marked as uncertain.
frames.verify_notes: Map III county trace released with explicit exact, possible, ambiguous, unreadable, and unfilled states.

frames.title: Holding companies reach most counties
frames.body: Holding-company groups operated across most of the country by 1932. Only 195 counties were blank on the federal map, down from 1,173 in 1925. Samuel Insull's system operated in 32 of the 48 states. Sixteen systems produced about three quarters of investor-owned electricity. Middle West Utilities entered receivership that April.
frames.note: This is a hand trace of Federal Trade Commission Map IV. Some counties also carry a number naming the operating utility inside the larger group. The source omits separately served cities. Unclear hatch patterns remain marked as uncertain.
frames.verify_notes: Map IV county trace released with explicit exact, possible, ambiguous, unreadable and unfilled states, an expanded machine-checked anchor set, and a published residual error estimate.

frames.title: Federal law breaks up utility holding companies
frames.body: Roosevelt signed the Public Utility Act on August 26, 1935. One part forced the layered holding companies to simplify. Another gave the federal government authority over interstate electricity sales. Texas utilities separated their system from Oklahoma. That decision helped create today's Texas grid.
frames.note: Federal jurisdiction can follow a synchronized grid even when one utility has no wire crossing a state line. Courts settled that principle decades later.

frames.title: Eastern and Western grids connect
frames.body: The map colors the Eastern and Western grids as one system. In February 1967, federal engineers closed several connections in Montana and Nebraska. Both grids began running in sync for the first time. Earlier tests had lasted only minutes or hours. This connection held for months.
frames.note: The connection remained unstable. Utilities opened it in July, closed it again in December, and watched it separate 381 times over the next eight months. The Texas grid remained separate throughout.

legend.label: East and West, running in step
The East-West divide, closed this year

frames.title: East and West separate again
frames.body: Utilities opened the unstable connections between East and West. The country returned to three synchronized grids: Eastern, Western, and Texas. No electricity crossed the East-West boundary in 1975. The blank boundary on this map represents a physical separation.
frames.note: The first converter station opened at Stegall, Nebraska, in 1977. It allowed limited power transfers without forcing both grids to run in sync. Later stations added more crossings.

legend.label: East-West boundary with no active crossing

frames.title: Independent market operators emerge
frames.body: The colors now show wholesale markets instead of synchronized grids. A 1996 federal order required transmission owners to give competitors equal access to their high-voltage lines. It encouraged independent operators without requiring utilities to join one. Five regional operators were running by the end of 1999.
frames.note: Texas and California created operators under state orders. Existing power pools in PJM, New England, and New York reorganized under federal rules. Most of the country still had no regional operator.

frames.title: Regional markets expand
frames.body: Each color shows the utilities participating in one wholesale market. PJM expanded west through Chicago, Ohio, Pittsburgh, and Virginia. MISO opened its five-minute energy market in 2005. Southwest Power Pool also became a regional market operator. The markets now covered much of the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic.
frames.note: Membership could change. Two Kentucky utilities left MISO in 2006. Ohio utilities moved from MISO to PJM in 2011 and 2012, shifting the market boundary several hundred miles west.

frames.title: MISO expands to the Gulf Coast
frames.body: Twelve utilities joined MISO on December 19, 2013. Its wholesale market had stretched from Minnesota to Indiana. It now reached the Gulf of Mexico through a southern region separated from the northern territory. Southwest Power Pool opened its own integrated market three months later.
frames.note: The frame is labeled 2014 because Southwest Power Pool opened its integrated market in March of that year. MISO's southern expansion occurred in December 2013.

frames.label: Today
frames.title: Seven markets across three physical grids
frames.body: The colors show seven regional market operators. About a third of the country has none. Under this market map, the United States still has three synchronized grids: Eastern, Western, and ERCOT. East and West exchange limited power through converter stations. ERCOT remains mostly separate inside Texas.
frames.note: This frame uses the same data as the Markets layer. The earlier frames explain how the physical grids and wholesale markets formed.

dots.note: The 27th largest city in the country, and today it is Pittsburgh's North Side. Pittsburgh annexed it in 1907 over the objections of its own voters.
Boston, Cambridge, Somerville and Lynn are four separate cities on this map because they were four separate cities, each buying its own light.

pearl-street-1882.title: Pearl Street switches on
pearl-street-1882.body: Edison's station in lower Manhattan started up with about 85 customers and roughly 400 lamps. It served the First District, a quarter of a square mile between Wall Street and the East River. Low-voltage direct current could not reach much past that without costing more in copper than the electricity was worth.
pearl-street-1882.note: This was the first Edison station to sell electricity in the United States. His Holborn Viaduct station in London opened earlier that year. The 1902 Census report shows an engraving of Pearl Street.

appleton-1882.title: A water wheel in Wisconsin
appleton-1882.body: A water-driven Edison dynamo on the Fox River at Appleton lit a paper mill and a house. It could run about 250 lamps. Customers paid a flat monthly fee per lamp, because nobody had invented a meter for this yet.
appleton-1882.note: This was the first hydroelectric station using Edison's incandescent system for paying customers. Grand Rapids had sold water-powered arc lighting since 1880. The 1902 Census caption uses the broader phrase “first Edison station.”

great-barrington-1886.title: Alternating current works
great-barrington-1886.body: William Stanley lit about twenty shops and offices along Main Street in Great Barrington. He sent alternating current down the street at 500 volts. Transformers in the basements reduced it to 100 volts for use. Modern grids still raise voltage for travel and lower it for customers.
great-barrington-1886.note: Stanley ran this experiment from an old rubber mill and shut it down that summer. The town's permanent electric utility arrived two years later.

telluride-1891.title: Power sent over a mountain
telluride-1891.body: The Ames plant sent alternating current 2.6 miles through the San Juan Mountains at 3,000 volts. The electricity powered a 100-horsepower motor at the Gold King mine. This was the first system to generate, transmit, and use alternating current for an industrial motor.
telluride-1891.note: Sources disagree on the day. June 19 is most common, while one local account gives June 21. Longer alternating-current lines already existed at Willamette Falls in Oregon. The industrial motor made Ames distinct.

niagara-buffalo-1896.title: Niagara reaches Buffalo
niagara-buffalo-1896.body: Just after midnight, 1,000 horsepower from a single generator at the falls travelled 26 miles at 11,000 volts to Buffalo, where it ran the city's street railway. After this, a power station no longer had to sit inside the city it served.
niagara-buffalo-1896.note: The first current went down the line at 8:57 that Sunday evening and reached Buffalo one minute after midnight, which met a contract deadline of on or before November 15.

pjm-pool-1927.title: Utilities form a power pool
pjm-pool-1927.body: Philadelphia Electric, Pennsylvania Power and Light, and Public Service of New Jersey connected their systems. They agreed to coordinate their power plants as one pool. It became North America's first large integrated high-voltage power pool. PJM still carries their initials.
pjm-pool-1927.note: Connecticut and Massachusetts utilities had shared power in 1922. The PJM pool integrated operations on a larger scale and continued running.

insull-collapse-1932.title: Middle West Utilities enters receivership
insull-collapse-1932.body: A federal judge in Chicago placed Middle West Utilities into receivership. It was the largest receivership in American business history at the time. The company could not pay $10 million in notes due June 1. Samuel Insull became one of three court-appointed receivers.
insull-collapse-1932.note: The holding companies failed while their operating utilities kept delivering electricity. Service continued across the system's 32 states.

northeast-blackout-1965.title: The lights go out in the Northeast
northeast-blackout-1965.body: A relay at a station in Ontario tripped. The disturbance spread through connected systems, and about 30 million people lost electricity across the Northeast. Large interconnections allowed one failure to travel farther.

golden-spike-1967.title: Eastern and Western grids synchronize
golden-spike-1967.body: Federal engineers closed several connections in Montana and western Nebraska. The Eastern and Western grids began running in sync. Earlier tests in 1957, 1962, and 1963 had lasted only minutes or hours. The February 1967 connection held for months.
golden-spike-1967.verify_notes: The exact number and location of the ties is contested. One archival account says four were planned, two in each state; the Federal Power Commission's own 1970 survey counts three in early 1967. The card hedges to a handful on purpose.
golden-spike-1967.note: Oscillations grew through the spring, so utilities opened the connections in late July. They closed them again on December 3. The grids separated automatically 381 times over the next eight months. ERCOT remained separate throughout.

nerc-1968.title: Utilities create reliability rules
nerc-1968.body: After the 1965 blackout, the industry created a council to write reliability rules. Nine regional groups operated under it. Compliance remained voluntary until 2007.
nerc-1968.note: The Federal Power Commission's 1970 survey dates this to 1969, against the council's own 1968.

purpa-1978.title: Independent generators gain market access
purpa-1978.body: The Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act required new federal rules for small independent generators. Utilities had to sell electricity to qualifying generators and buy electricity from them. Utilities could no longer refuse every transaction.
purpa-1978.note: The price was capped at what the utility would have spent making the power itself. The 80 megawatt size limit applied only to small power producers, not to cogeneration.

epact-1992.title: Congress permits wholesale competition
epact-1992.body: The Energy Policy Act allowed independent generators to sell electricity in wholesale markets. It also allowed them to request access to utility-owned transmission lines. Transmission owners still controlled whether access worked in practice.

order-888-1996.title: Transmission opens to competitors
order-888-1996.body: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ordered transmission owners to publish open-access prices and terms. Competitors could move wholesale electricity over the same lines on the same terms as the owner. The order described independent operators without requiring utilities to create one.

ercot-iso-1996.title: Texas designates an independent operator
ercot-iso-1996.body: Texas regulators designated ERCOT as an independent system operator. It began that role in September 1996. Ten utility control areas continued operating the physical grid until ERCOT combined them into one control area on July 31, 2001.

caiso-1998.title: California opens wholesale trading
caiso-1998.body: California's independent grid operator and power exchange began wholesale trading. The state also opened retail electricity sales. A severe market crisis two years later led California to restrict retail choice.
caiso-1998.note: California's regulators had ordered an operator into existence in December 1995, before Order 888 issued.

nyiso-1999.title: New York creates the fifth operator
nyiso-1999.body: New York's independent operator took over from the power pool formed after the 1965 blackout. Five regional operators were now running in Texas, New England, PJM, California, and New York. Most of the country remained outside them.

order-2000-1999.title: Federal regulators request regional operator plans
order-2000-1999.body: Order 2000 required every transmission owner to file a proposal for a regional operator or explain its progress toward joining one. The filing was mandatory. Membership remained voluntary. About a third of the country still has no regional market operator.

comed-2004.title: Chicago joins PJM
comed-2004.body: Commonwealth Edison joined PJM. Its Chicago territory sat about 300 miles west of PJM's existing market, creating a temporary island on the map.

aep-dayton-2004.title: AEP and Dayton join PJM
aep-dayton-2004.body: Seven American Electric Power utilities and Dayton Power and Light joined PJM on the same day. Their territories connected Chicago to PJM's eastern region. PJM became the country's largest wholesale market.

dominion-2005.title: Virginia joins PJM
dominion-2005.body: Dominion joined PJM. Its Virginia territory extended the market to the Atlantic coast south of Washington, DC.

miso-market-2005.title: MISO starts trading
miso-market-2005.body: MISO opened a wholesale energy market that calculates prices every five minutes. It had begun coordinating reliability in December 2001 and billing for transmission service in February 2002.
miso-market-2005.note: MISO took on different functions at different times. Transmission billing began in 2002. The five-minute energy market began in 2005.

spp-nebraska-2009.title: Nebraska joins SPP
spp-nebraska-2009.body: Nebraska's major public utilities joined Southwest Power Pool. Nebraska is the only state where every electricity utility is publicly owned.

miso-south-2013.title: MISO reaches the Gulf
miso-south-2013.body: Entergy's six operating utilities and six neighboring companies joined MISO at midnight on December 19. The market expanded from the Upper Midwest to the Gulf of Mexico. Its new southern region did not touch the northern territory.
miso-south-2013.note: After the expansion, MISO reported 65,280 miles of transmission and about 196,000 megawatts of generating capacity across 15 states and Manitoba. Entergy had previously run its own control area outside any regional market.

integrated-system-2015.title: The federal dams join a market
integrated-system-2015.body: Western Area Power Administration's Upper Great Plains system, Basin Electric, and Heartland joined Southwest Power Pool. Their membership brought electricity from federal Missouri River dams into the regional market.

spp-west-2026.title: SPP opens a western market
spp-west-2026.body: A group of western utilities opened a second wholesale market run by Southwest Power Pool. SPP now operates markets on both the Eastern and Western grids across parts of 17 states. The physical grids remain separate.

caldwell-2026.title: A town changes grids
caldwell-2026.body: Caldwell, Texas, had been a small Eastern-grid island inside the ERCOT region. New transmission lines connected the city to ERCOT in March 2026.

insull-empire-1930.title: Insull's system reaches 32 states
insull-empire-1930.body: Samuel Insull's Middle West Utilities controlled more than 85 utility companies. The Federal Trade Commission found that the group operated in 32 states and Canada at the end of 1930. It served more than 5,000 communities with over 6.5 million residents.
insull-empire-1930.note: The system expanded quickly. Company reports named 15 states in 1923 and 29 in 1929. Each figure on this map keeps the year of its source.

ebasco-1930.title: Electric Bond and Share reaches 32 states
ebasco-1930.body: General Electric created Electric Bond and Share in 1905. By the early 1930s it was the country's largest utility holding company. Five subholding companies sat beneath it. Those companies controlled roughly 237 subsidiaries.
ebasco-1930.note: The Supreme Court recorded operations in 32 states. That count includes American Gas and Electric, which Bond and Share influenced through a minority stake. The number depends on how the source defines control.

concentration-1930.title: Sixteen systems produce three quarters of the power
concentration-1930.body: The Federal Trade Commission counted electricity generated by sixteen holding-company systems. They produced 75.8% of all investor-owned electricity in 1930. The same table reports 80.2% in 1929 and 76.4% in 1932.
concentration-1930.note: The commission said these percentages understated corporate control because small voting stakes could still produce control. The records use different denominators and sometimes count the same electricity twice, so the individual systems cannot be added or ranked cleanly.

ftc-investigation-1928.title: Congress orders an investigation
ftc-investigation-1928.body: Senate Resolution 83 ordered the Federal Trade Commission to investigate utility holding companies. The commission examined their ownership, finances, and operations for years. The final record filled 95 printed volumes.

public-utility-act-1935.title: Roosevelt signs the Public Utility Act
public-utility-act-1935.body: Roosevelt signed the Public Utility Act of 1935. Title I forced utility holding companies to simplify. Title II became the Federal Power Act and gave a federal commission authority over interstate electricity sales. Both sections still shape the map.
public-utility-act-1935.note: Congress cited the Federal Trade Commission investigation. Section 11(b)(2) limited the corporate stack: one company could sit above a holding company, while deeper holding-company layers had to go.

texas-opens-switches-1935.title: Texas utilities disconnect from Oklahoma
texas-opens-switches-1935.body: Two Texas utilities opened their connections to Oklahoma before the new federal law took effect. Keeping their synchronized system inside one state reduced federal jurisdiction. Other Texas utilities followed the same strategy. It helped create today's separate ERCOT grid.
texas-opens-switches-1935.note: The separation remained incomplete in 1935. Wartime connections and later court cases tested whether Texas had stayed outside interstate electricity sales.

texas-interconnects.title: Texas utilities connect to each other
texas-interconnects.body: Texas utilities had begun connecting their systems by 1924. A northern group formed first. A southern group expanded during World War II as utilities shared power for wartime factories. A statewide system emerged informally in the early 1940s and gained a formal organization in 1967.
texas-interconnects.note: Shipyards, refineries, steel mills, a magnesium plant, and aircraft factories increased wartime electricity needs. Texas manufacturing output roughly quadrupled between 1939 and 1944.
texas-interconnects.verify_notes: The load driver is sourced as the scale of the buildout, not as an electricity figure. Do not restate it as demand growth without a source.

puhca-breakup.title: Holding companies simplify
puhca-breakup.body: The Securities and Exchange Commission enforced the 1935 law by simplifying utility holding companies. Their operating utilities became many of the regional companies known today. Major restructurings occurred between 1945 and 1950.

wscc-1967.title: Western utilities form a council
wscc-1967.body: Western utilities created a coordinating council in 1967. It covered the full Western grid and developed regional reliability practices.

ac-ties-opened.title: East and West separate again
ac-ties-opened.body: Utilities opened the unstable alternating-current connections between the Eastern and Western grids. The lines remained in place without carrying power. The country returned to three synchronized grids: Eastern, Western, and Texas. No active connection crossed the East-West boundary in 1975.

stegall-1977.title: A converter reconnects East and West
stegall-1977.body: A cooperative opened a 100-megawatt converter station at Stegall, Nebraska. It converted alternating current to direct current and back. Electricity could cross while the Eastern and Western grids continued running separately.
stegall-1977.note: Some later accounts identify the 1988 Virginia Smith station as the first East-West converter. Its engineering award does not make that claim. The Stegall record dates this earlier connection to 1977.

midnight-connection-1976.title: A midnight connection tests Texas
midnight-connection-1976.body: A Texas utility briefly closed a switch to Oklahoma in the middle of the night. The connection synchronized part of Texas with the Eastern grid. It triggered a legal fight over federal authority that continued through 1979.
midnight-connection-1976.note: The dispute shows that Texas utilities understood and deliberately maintained the grid's separation.

iso-ne-1997.title: ISO New England begins operating
iso-ne-1997.body: ISO New England took over regional coordination from the power pool shared by six New England states since 1971.

pjm-iso-1997.title: PJM becomes an independent operator
pjm-iso-1997.body: Federal regulators approved the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland power pool's plan to become an independent operator. PJM began the new role on January 1, 1998. Its member utilities had proposed the change.
pjm-iso-1997.note: PJM gained provisional regional transmission organization status in July 2001 and full approval in December 2002.

spp-rto-2004.title: Southwest Power Pool becomes a regional market operator
spp-rto-2004.body: A power pool that had coordinated central utilities since World War II became a regional transmission organization. The new status formalized its independent role under federal rules.

duquesne-2005.title: Duquesne joins PJM
duquesne-2005.body: Duquesne Light, the utility serving Pittsburgh, joined PJM. It later received approval to move to MISO. A 2009 settlement kept the utility in PJM.

lge-ku-2006.title: Two Kentucky utilities leave MISO
lge-ku-2006.body: Louisville Gas and Electric and Kentucky Utilities left MISO after four years. Their net exit payment was about $27 million. Both have remained outside a regional wholesale market.

atsi-2011.title: FirstEnergy switches markets
atsi-2011.body: Three FirstEnergy utilities in Ohio moved from MISO to PJM after nearly eight years. Their transfer shifted the wholesale market boundary several hundred miles west.

deok-2012.title: Duke utilities move to PJM
deok-2012.body: Duke Energy Ohio and Duke Energy Kentucky moved from MISO to PJM at the start of 2012. Their transfer continued the market boundary's westward shift.

nerc-enforceable-2007.title: Reliability rules become enforceable
nerc-enforceable-2007.body: Federal law made the industry's reliability rules enforceable. The 2005 Energy Policy Act created the authority. Federal regulators certified the reliability organization in 2006 and approved 83 standards in March 2007. The standards took effect that June.

spp-marketplace-2014.title: SPP opens its integrated market
spp-marketplace-2014.body: Southwest Power Pool launched its Integrated Marketplace. It also combined participating utility control areas into one regional balancing authority that day.

lubbock-2023.title: A city changes grids
lubbock-2023.body: Lubbock moved its local system from the Eastern grid into ERCOT. About 70% of the city's electricity demand moved in 2021, and the remaining connection finished in December 2023. Households gained the ability to choose a seller in March 2024.

dc-ties-today.title: Converters link the Eastern and Western grids
dc-ties-today.body: About seven converter stations connect the Eastern and Western grids. Together they can transfer roughly 1,300 megawatts. Both grids serve hundreds of thousands of megawatts, so the connection remains small relative to their size.
dc-ties-today.note: Sources count six or seven stations depending on how they classify one site. Adding nameplate ratings also overstates the power that can move at the same time.

ercot-federal-reach.title: ERCOT remains mostly under Texas authority
ercot-federal-reach.body: ERCOT is the only major synchronized grid contained within one state. It carries about 90% of Texas electricity. El Paso, the Panhandle, and part of East Texas use the other two grids. Staying within Texas limits federal authority over rates and transmission service.
ercot-federal-reach.note: ERCOT still follows federal reliability law. It pays reliability-organization fees, undergoes regional audits, and remains subject to specific federal transmission powers. Only Alaska and Hawaii are exempt from the federal reliability statute.

pacific-intertie.title: The Pacific Intertie connects north and south
pacific-intertie.body: The Pacific direct-current intertie runs from the Columbia River region to Los Angeles. It carries surplus hydroelectricity south during spring runoff and can send other power north during winter demand.
pacific-intertie.verify_notes: Length, voltage and capacity were all corrected during research and the figures have grown over time with upgrades. Do not print a capacity without checking which year it belongs to.

puhca-1935.label: The 1935 Act, section 11(b)(2)
puhca-1935.citation: Public Utility Act of 1935, ch. 687, 49 Stat. 803, section 11(b)(2).
puhca-1935.quote: cease to be a holding company with respect to each of its subsidiary companies which itself has a subsidiary company which is a holding company
puhca-1935.gloss: The law allowed one corporate layer above a holding company. Deeper holding-company stacks had to be removed.
puhca-1935.note: This quotation comes directly from section 11(b)(2) of the enacted law.

purpa-1978.label: PURPA, 1978, section 210
purpa-1978.citation: Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978, 92 Stat. 3144, section 210(a).
purpa-1978.quote: the Commission shall prescribe, and from time to time thereafter revise, such rules as it determines necessary to encourage cogeneration and small power production which rules require electric utilities to offer to (1) sell electric energy to qualifying cogeneration facilities and qualifying small power production facilities and (2) purchase electric energy from such facilities
purpa-1978.gloss: Utilities had to buy electricity from qualifying independent generators and sell electricity to them when needed.

order-888-1996.label: FERC Order 888, 1996
order-888-1996.citation: FERC Order No. 888, Docket Nos. RM95-8-000 and RM94-7-001, issued April 24, 1996.
order-888-1996.quote: issuing a Final Rule requiring all public utilities that own, control or operate facilities used for transmitting electric energy in interstate commerce to have on file open access non-discriminatory transmission tariffs that contain minimum terms and conditions of non-discriminatory service
order-888-1996.gloss: Transmission owners had to offer competitors the same access terms they used themselves. The order described independent operators without requiring one.

order-2000-1999.label: FERC Order 2000, 1999
order-2000-1999.citation: FERC Order No. 2000, Docket No. RM99-2-000, issued December 20, 1999.
order-2000-1999.quote: all public utilities... that own, operate or control interstate transmission facilities must file with the Commission by October 15, 2000, a proposal for an RTO... or, alternatively, a description of efforts to participate in an RTO, any existing obstacles to RTO participation, and any plans to work toward RTO participation
order-2000-1999.gloss: Transmission owners had to propose a regional operator or explain their progress toward joining one. Membership remained voluntary.

census-1902-stations.title: Central Electric Light and Power Stations, 1902
census-1902-stations.citation: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Special Reports: Central Electric Light and Power Stations, 1902. Government Printing Office, 1905. Public domain.
census-1902-stations.note: The first national count found 3,620 central power stations. Companies owned 2,805 and towns owned 815. Three quarters served places with fewer than 5,000 residents. The report excludes private plants built by factories and hotels.

ftc-72a-map3-fields-of-operation-1925.title: Map III: fields of operations of principal power groups, by county, 1925
ftc-72a-map3-fields-of-operation-1925.citation: Federal Trade Commission, Utility Corporations, Summary Report on Economic, Financial, and Corporate Phases of Holding and Operating Companies of Electric and Gas Utilities, S. Doc. No. 92, pt. 72-A, 70th Cong., 1st Sess. (1935), map III, opposite p. 56.
ftc-72a-map3-fields-of-operation-1925.rights: United States federal government publication, public domain
ftc-72a-map3-fields-of-operation-1925.note: The map uses hatch patterns to show which major holding-company group operated utilities in each county. It is the source for the interactive 1925 county layer.

ftc-72a-map4-fields-of-operation-1932.title: Map IV: fields of operations of principal power groups, by county, 1932
ftc-72a-map4-fields-of-operation-1932.citation: Federal Trade Commission, Utility Corporations, Summary Report on Economic, Financial, and Corporate Phases of Holding and Operating Companies of Electric and Gas Utilities, S. Doc. No. 92, pt. 72-A, 70th Cong., 1st Sess. (1935), map IV, opposite p. 56.
ftc-72a-map4-fields-of-operation-1932.rights: United States federal government publication, public domain
ftc-72a-map4-fields-of-operation-1932.note: The 1932 map uses hatch patterns to show major holding-company operations. It is the source for the interactive 1932 county layer. Its printed note says separately served cities and towns are omitted, and uncertain county readings stay marked as uncertain.

ftc-72a-map1-transmission-lines-1932.title: Electric transmission lines by holding-company group, 1932
ftc-72a-map1-transmission-lines-1932.citation: Federal Trade Commission, Utility Corporations, S. Doc. No. 92, pt. 72-A, 70th Cong., 1st Sess. (1935), map I, opposite p. 40.
ftc-72a-map1-transmission-lines-1932.rights: United States federal government publication, public domain
ftc-72a-map1-transmission-lines-1932.note: This national map assigns high-voltage transmission lines to holding-company groups. It shows the physical grid growing beneath the corporate empires.

ftc-72a-table12-generation-by-group.title: Table 12: Electric energy generated by holding company groups, large local companies and small local companies, 1929, 1930 and 1932
ftc-72a-table12-generation-by-group.citation: Federal Trade Commission, Utility Corporations, S. Doc. No. 92, pt. 72-A, 70th Cong., 1st Sess. (1935), table 12, p. 38.

ftc-72a-table19-operating-companies-by-g.title: Table 19: Assets, operating revenues and net income of 91 operating companies, by holding company group

puhca-statute-49-stat-803.title: Public Utility Act of 1935, ch. 687, 49 Stat. 803, first printed page
puhca-statute-49-stat-803.archive: govinfo (GPO), United States Statutes at Large
puhca-statute-49-stat-803.rights: United States federal government publication, public domain
puhca-statute-49-stat-803.note: The opening page dates the law to August 26, 1935. Section 1(b) states that Congress acted on the Federal Trade Commission investigation ordered by Senate Resolution 83.

puhca-section-11-49-stat-820-821.title: Public Utility Holding Company Act, section 11
puhca-section-11-49-stat-820-821.archive: govinfo (GPO), United States Statutes at Large
puhca-section-11-49-stat-820-821.rights: United States federal government publication, public domain
puhca-section-11-49-stat-820-821.note: Section 11(b)(1) limited each holding company to an integrated utility system. Section 11(b)(2) removed deeper layers of holding companies from the corporate stack.

ftc-annual-report-1938-volume-list.title: Federal Trade Commission account of the investigation, 1938
ftc-annual-report-1938-volume-list.archive: FRASER, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
ftc-annual-report-1938-volume-list.quote: are included in 84 printed volumes which, with 11 summary, final, index and appendix volumes, or a total of 95 were published as Senate Document No. 92, Seventieth Congress, first session, under the general title, Utility Corporations. … During the Investigation, the Commission's accountants, engineers, and economists examined 29 holding companies having total assets of $6,108,128,713; 70 subholding companies with total assets of $5,685,463,201, and 278 operating companies with total assets of $7,245,106,464.
ftc-annual-report-1938-volume-list.note: The commission reported 95 printed volumes and examinations of 377 holding, subholding, and operating companies. Congress cited this investigation in the 1935 law.

fpc-1964-nps-principal-transmission-1962.citation: United States. Federal Power Commission. National Power Survey: A Report. Part I. Washington: U.S. Government Printing Office, October 1964, p. 210, Figures 113 and 114. Internet Archive identifier nationalpowersur00unit.
fpc-1964-nps-principal-transmission-1962.rights: Public domain in the United States as a work of the US Government (17 U.S.C. 105). Author on title page: United States. Federal Power Commission. archive.org supplies no rights statement for this item, so the public-domain basis is statutory rather than asserted by the archive. fpc-1964-nps-1980-projection-west.title: Projected 1980 transmission and generation pattern, western half (Figure 116)

fpc-1970-nps-regions-and-power-supply-ar.archive: Internet Archive (Bureau of Land Management Library scan)

fpc-1970-nps-regions-and-power-supply-ar.note: This federal survey divides the country into six planning regions and 48 numbered power-supply areas. It shows how planners organized the national system before today's regional markets existed.

fpc-1970-nps-transmission-system-figure-.rights: Public domain, US Government work. Same credit as Figure 3.6.
fpc-1970-nps-transmission-system-figure-.note: This two-page map shows the 1970 high-voltage transmission system. Line color and pattern distinguish voltage levels and direct-current links. It documents the physical network around the time East and West separated again.

EASTERN.name: The Eastern grid
EASTERN.body: The Eastern grid reaches from the Atlantic to a boundary through Montana, the Dakotas, Nebraska, and eastern New Mexico. Generators across this area run in sync, making it one physical system.
EASTERN.note: It is the largest of the three synchronized grids in the continental United States.

WESTERN.name: The Western grid
WESTERN.body: The Western grid reaches from the East-West boundary to the Pacific and includes parts of Canada and Mexico. Its generators run in sync with each other and separately from the Eastern grid.

ERCOT.name: The Texas grid
ERCOT.body: The ERCOT grid covers most of Texas. Texas utilities maintained a separate synchronized system after the 1935 expansion of federal authority over interstate electricity sales.
ERCOT.note: The grid does not follow the state border. El Paso uses the Western grid. Amarillo, Beaumont, and other areas use the Eastern grid.
